utterance: Hi Daniel, I'm the doctor. I understand you've hurt your lower back lifting something over the weekend — that sounds really painful. Before we talk about scans and treatment, let me get a clear picture of what happened. Can you tell me what you were doing when it happened, and what the pain felt like at that moment?
reply: I was lifting a big pot plant in the garden on Saturday. I felt a twinge, then woke up Sunday and could barely get out of bed. The pain is low down on the left side of my back, sometimes into my left buttock. It's worse when I bend or get out of a chair, better when lying still with a heat pack, and gets worse by the evening. I've been working from home the last two days, mostly lying on the couch with the laptop. I can walk around slowly.

utterance: Thanks, that's helpful. A few important questions now. Does the pain travel below your buttock — into your thigh, calf or foot? And do you have any numbness, tingling, pins-and-needles, or weakness in either leg — for example, foot dragging or difficulty lifting your toes?
reply: No, nothing down my legs. My legs feel completely normal — no numbness, tingling, pins-and-needles, or weakness. I can walk around slowly and don’t have any difficulty lifting my toes.

awards.label: Whether the pain spreads down the legs
Red flag excluded: Weakness, numbness or pins and needles in the legs

utterance: Good — that's reassuring. Now some key safety questions I ask everyone with back pain. Any problems controlling your bladder or bowels — difficulty passing urine, leaking, or trouble controlling your bowel movements? Any numbness or strange sensation in the area between your legs or around your back passage?
reply: No, I haven't had any problems controlling my bladder or bowels — no difficulty passing urine, leaking, or trouble with bowel movements. I don't have any numbness or strange sensations around my back passage or between my legs.

awards.label: Red flag excluded: Any change in passing urine — difficulty, retention or leaking
Red flag excluded: Any loss of bowel control
Red flag excluded: Numbness around the buttocks, genitals or back passage

utterance: Great, that's reassuring too. A few more general health questions: have you had any fever, chills, or night sweats? Any unexplained weight loss recently? Any history of cancer, and do you take steroid tablets or have any conditions affecting your bones? Have you ever used intravenous drugs or had a recent infection anywhere?
reply: No fever, chills or night sweats. I've put on a bit of weight recently. No history of cancer. I don't take steroids or have any bone conditions. Never used intravenous drugs and haven't had any recent infections.

utterance: Understood. Have you had back pain like this before, or is this the first time? What have you taken or tried so far for the pain? I see on your file you had a bad reaction to tramadol — vomiting and dizziness — so we'll steer well clear of that.
reply: This is the first time I've had back pain like this — I tweaked my back maybe five years ago, but it was gone in a week. I've only taken some paracetamol, but it didn't do much, honestly. I know I had a bad reaction to tramadol before — vomiting and dizziness — so I'll make sure to avoid that.

utterance:
Thanks, Daniel. My examination backs up what you described: the muscles alongside your lower spine are in spasm and tender, your back movement is limited by pain, but your leg nerves, strength, sensation and reflexes are all completely normal. This looks like a classic muscle strain from the lifting — often called acute mechanical low back pain.

Before I talk about treatment and the MRI question, a few quick safety questions so I can choose the right anti-inflammatory for you: do you have any history of stomach ulcers, bad reflux, kidney problems, high blood pressure, heart problems, or asthma? Do you take any blood-thinning medicines?
reply: No, I don't have a history of stomach ulcers or bad reflux, but I do have asthma. My kidneys are fine as far as I know, and I don't have high blood pressure, heart problems or any blood-thinning medicines.

awards.label: Stomach ulcers or indigestion with anti-inflammatories
Kidney problems
Asthma

utterance: One more thing about the asthma, because some anti-inflammatory tablets (NSAIDs, like Nurofen/ibuprofen or naproxen) can trigger wheezing in a small number of people with asthma. Have you ever taken ibuprofen or similar anti-inflammatories before? Did your asthma flare, or was it fine? And is your asthma generally well controlled at the moment — do you use a preventer or just a reliever inhaler?
reply: I’ve never taken ibuprofen or similar anti-inflammatories before, so I don’t know if my asthma would have flared. I use a preventer inhaler most days.

awards.label: Naproxen or celecoxib as the NSAID

utterance:
I've prescribed you naproxen 500 mg twice a day with food for 5 days — it's an anti-inflammatory that works much better than paracetamol for this kind of injury, and it also eases the muscle spasm. Two important things about it: take it with or straight after food, and stop it immediately and use your asthma inhaler if you notice any wheezing or breathing trouble — that would mean your asthma doesn't like this type of medicine and you should tell me. If your stomach gets upset, stop it too. Don't take ibuprofen or Nurofen on top of it — it's the same family.

Now, about the MRI — I want to explain why I don't think it's the right move today. Your story and my examination show a muscle strain with absolutely no signs of nerve damage or anything serious — normal strength, sensation, reflexes, and normal bladder and bowel. Guidelines in Australia are very clear: for back pain like this in the first 6 weeks, an MRI doesn't help — it doesn't change treatment, it doesn't make you recover faster, and it very often shows "wear and tear" changes that are normal in 40-year-olds and have nothing to do with your pain. People who get scans for ordinary back strain actually tend to do worse, because the findings can lead to unnecessary worry and interventions. Most people with this improve a lot within 1–2 weeks and fully within 4–6 weeks.

The plan: keep moving — gentle walking several times a day, avoid bed rest and long stretches lying on the couch (that actually stiffens it up more), keep working as you can, keep using your heat pack, and let pain be your guide — soreness is fine, sharp worsening pain means ease off. Would you like a physiotherapy referral for a few sessions? It can help with pain relief and getting you moving again, and they can tailor exercises for you.
reply: I understand the MRI isn't needed right now — the pain seems to be from a muscle strain, and there's no nerve damage. I just wanted to know what's going on, and I'm happy to try the naproxen and follow the plan. A physiotherapy referral would be good, though — I want to get back to normal as quickly as possible.

awards.label: What he expects from the visit
Physiotherapy referral

utterance:
Done — you're booked in with a physiotherapist, and they'll help you with hands-on relief and a graded exercise plan to get you back to normal quickly.

Here's when I need to see you again or when you need urgent care, so please remember these red flags. Come back to me — or go straight to hospital if it's severe — if you develop:
- any loss of control of your bladder or bowels, or trouble starting urination
- numbness between your legs or around your back passage
- new weakness in a leg, like a foot slapping the ground when you walk
- fever with the back pain
- pain that's relentlessly worse at night despite lying still, or you feel generally unwell.

And for the ordinary course: if you're not clearly improving over the next 2 weeks, or you're still substantially limited by 4–6 weeks, come back and we'll reassess — and at that point imaging and other options are much more meaningful. If the naproxen causes any wheezing, stop it and let me know.

Any questions about any of that before we finish?
reply: No, I don't have any questions. I just wanted to mention that I've been reading about slipped discs and people needing surgery — but I understand that's not the case here. I'll follow the plan and keep you updated.

awards.label: What he is worried the pain might be
Defensible diagnosis: Mechanical low back pain
Reasonable differential: Lumbar disc prolapse with sciatica
Reasonable differential: Cauda equina syndrome
Can't-miss diagnosis considered: Cauda equina syndrome

utterance:
That's a very common worry, so let me reassure you clearly: a "slipped disc" pressing on a nerve usually causes pain, numbness or weakness shooting down a leg below the knee — and you have none of that. Your leg nerves checked out completely normal today. And even when a disc does bulge, the vast majority heal on their own without surgery. Only a tiny fraction ever need an operation, and we'd only even discuss it if there was persistent, significant nerve damage over many weeks.

To recap the plan: naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food for 5 days (stop if any wheezing or stomach upset), heat packs, gentle movement and walking — no bed rest, physio referral booked, work as tolerated. Watch for the red flags we discussed — any bladder or bowel changes, numbness between the legs, leg weakness or fever means urgent review or hospital. If you're not improving within 2 weeks or still limited at 4–6 weeks, come back and we'll reassess.

Thanks, Daniel — take care, and I hope the back settles quickly.
reply: Thanks, I'll take care and follow the plan. I just wanted to mention that I'll keep you updated if anything changes — especially if the pain gets worse or if I notice any new symptoms.
